More than 1,300 people are missing in Nepal and Tibet, including 47 Americans, after a glacial collapse caused catastrophic floods, with video showing mud sweeping through entire communities. Drone footage in Nepal showed roads destroyed and buildings buried by thundering water the color of wet cement. Nepalese authorities ramped up operations in the worst-affected districts of Nuwakot and Rasuwa. The disaster in Nepal and Tibet is not a one-off. The Lhende Khola river system has now flooded twice in just 14 months and the increasingly unstable Himalayan ice system threatens communities, infrastructure and water supplies across one of the world’s most densely populated regions. The region saw similar flash floods in August last year, when a glacial lake in Tibet overflowed because of high temperatures. Nine people were killed, and critical infrastructure, including a bridge connecting Nepal and China, was damaged.

Farmers with disabilities in rural Nepal are facing severe impacts from climate change as unpredictable rainfall, flooding, and soil erosion threaten their livelihoods. Limited mobility and resources make it even harder for them to recover from disasters. Organizations like COP must ensure climate policies support farmers with disabilities in adapting to a changing world. This is Part 2 of our series exploring the intersection of climate change and disability ahead of #COP29. [Video ID: Video clips showing flooding and landslides in Nepal. Text on screen says, “Germanwatch's 2021 Global Climate Risk Index assessed 180 countries' vulnerability to climate change. Nepal ranked 12th. Many Nepalis living in remote, mountainous regions make a living off farming. Increased soil erosion, drought, and flooding are threatening their livelihoods. Farmers with disabilities in rural Nepal are especially at risk because they face greater barriers to mobility, resources, and recovery efforts during climate disasters.” Amar Singh Bhandari, a farmer from the Humla District, speaks to camera: “Namaste, sir. I am from Ward No. 2, Sinkot Rural Municipality, formerly Ward No. 5. My name is Amar Singh Bhandari. I do farming for my livelihood. I have given education to my children. I am a person with a disabled leg. Whether it rains or snows, it never comes when we need it. It either pours continuously, or doesn’t come at all. I can’t carry heavy loads. If someone calls me disabled, it pains me. The impacts are endless.” Danlal Kami, another farmer from Humla, speaks to camera: “It hasn’t rained in Humla from October last year until August this year. Then, it rained nonstop since August 17 or 18 and damaged a lot of people’s houses. My two-story house was completely destroyed.” Text on screen says, “International groups like the United Nations Conference of the Parties (COP) can drive change by pushing for inclusive climate policies and ensuring that rural farmers with disabilities are included in climate adaptation and resilience efforts. Supporting farmers with disabilities in adapting to climate change ensures that no one is left behind in the fight for a sustainable future.”]

THE FLOOD LASTED HOURS. THE ECONOMIC DAMAGE COULD LAST YEARS. 🇳🇵 Nepal’s August 26 flash flood is no longer only a humanitarian disaster. It is becoming an economic and political crisis. 💰 $2.56 BILLION IN PRELIMINARY DAMAGE Initial assessments estimate approximately NPR 387.5 billion (US$2.56B) in direct damage to homes, roads, bridges, energy, agriculture and telecommunications. ⚡ HYDROPOWER HIT Around 281 MW of operating hydropower capacity and another 388 MW under construction were affected—significant for a country heavily dependent on hydropower. 🇨🇳 TRADE DISRUPTED Damage around Rasuwagadhi disrupted a critical Nepal–China trade corridor that handled more than $600M in trade in 2025. 🏠 THOUSANDS OF HOMES Preliminary assessments identified approximately 7,570 damaged homes, while commercial insurance losses could exceed NPR 20 billion (~US$132M). 🏛️ THE POLITICAL COST The government is facing pressure over disaster preparedness, rescue speed and coordination while thousands remain missing. Nepal has also requested international assistance for specialized rescue equipment and infrastructure. The water may disappear quickly. The economic and political consequences could remain for years. 🇳🇵
